deep.plain: Software used to be written line by line by programmers. Today you can describe what you want in normal language and an AI writes the code, tests it and fixes its own mistakes. The labs that build AI now use their own AI to write most of their code and to speed up their research. Think of a carpenter who builds a better saw, then uses that saw to build an even better one: each round goes faster.

terms.def: An AI that writes, runs and fixes code on its own, over many steps, rather than suggesting one line at a time.
Building software by describing what you want and accepting what the AI produces, with little or no reading of the code.
How long a task, measured in human working time, an AI agent can complete reliably on its own. METR tracks how fast this grows.

going.text: AI writes code, the code trains better AI, better AI writes better code. This is why progress feels like it keeps speeding up rather than levelling off.

METR, an independent evaluator, estimates the length of tasks agents complete reliably now doubles every three to four months (it was about seven). In November 2026 it estimated Anthropic’s model progress has run 1.9x faster since October 2025, mostly because AI helps the researchers.

Most new software builders are domain experts, not developers: a controller who builds a reconciliation tool, a planner who builds a scheduling app. The scarce skill moves from typing code to knowing what is worth building and checking that it works.

going.lead: A glimpse of AI editing AI
going.text: MIT researchers had one model directly edit 0.016% of another model’s internal settings and lifted its maths score from 7.9% to 48.1% with no retraining. Critics say it fixed a specific flaw rather than adding new skill, so treat it as a sign of direction, not a breakthrough.

deep.why: Anyone with domain knowledge can now build working software. Customers will expect prototypes in days, not quarters.
know: The 80% machine-written figure is Anthropic’s own internal number for its own code, not an industry average.
METR’s 1.9x covers one lab and has a wide range (1.5–2.8x). Disclosure: Anthropic makes Claude, which helped prepare this text.
Writing code faster is not the same as building the right thing. Review, testing and security still take human judgement.

qa.q: Does this mean we need fewer developers?
qa.a: It changes what developers do: more specifying, reviewing and integrating, less typing. Organisations are still working out the right team shape.
It is why labs and governments focus on testing and oversight. For business the point is speed: expect capability jumps more often.

deep.plain: An AI agent is software that doesn’t just answer a question but carries out a task: it plans steps, uses tools, and checks the result. The new step is agents handing work to other agents, like a project manager who delegates to specialists. A travel agent AI might ask a booking agent AI to reserve a flight and a finance agent AI to approve the cost. The ambition is huge; most companies are still stuck at the pilot stage.

terms.def: Software that pursues a goal over several steps, using tools such as search, email or company systems.
An open standard, introduced by Anthropic in 2024, that lets AI models connect to tools and data in a uniform way, like a universal plug.
An open protocol, introduced by Google in 2025, that lets agents from different vendors talk to and hand work to each other.
Coordinating many agents and systems so a whole business process runs end to end.

going.text: Protocols like MCP and A2A do for agents what HTTP did for websites: they let pieces built by different companies work together. That is what makes agent-to-agent work possible.

unclear ownership, missing integration with real processes, security and trust concerns, and no agreed way to measure success. Model quality is rarely the main blocker.

deep.why: Customers’ processes will increasingly run agent to agent. Whatever we sell has to be reachable by their agents, and we can help close the gap from pilot to production.
know: ‘Agent’ is used loosely in marketing; many products called agents are chatbots with a few tool connections.
Agent-to-agent chains multiply errors: if each step is 95% reliable, ten steps in a row are far less reliable.

qa.q: What’s the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
qa.a: A chatbot answers; an agent acts. It takes steps in other systems on your behalf.

qa.q: Why should a business care about agent protocols?
qa.a: If customers’ agents can’t read or call your services, you become invisible to automated buying and workflows.

deep.plain: For decades robots were big arms bolted to the floor, doing one job behind a safety fence. Humanoid robots are built in human shape so they can work in spaces designed for people, and AI lets them learn tasks instead of being programmed step by step. At the same time, driverless taxis have become a normal paid service in several US cities. Robots are leaving the lab and doing real shifts.

terms.def: A robot with a roughly human body plan (arms, legs or wheels, hands) so it can use human tools and spaces.
A taxi with no driver, operated by companies such as Waymo.
AI that perceives and acts in the physical world through a body, rather than only producing text or images.

going.text: Figure’s F.02 humanoids helped build more than 30,000 BMW X3s during an 11-month pilot at Spartanburg; Figure 03 robots now work in logistics there.
19,000–22,000 humanoids shipped worldwide in the first half of 2026, up roughly 270–300%, and over 97% came from Chinese vendors. Cheap hardware plus state support is scaling fast.
Waymo reports about 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US cities and targets 1 million a week by year-end.
better AI for perception and planning, cheaper batteries and motors, and world models (see ‘AI Learns the Physical World’) that let robots practise in simulation.

deep.why: Physical work is now in scope for AI. Customers in manufacturing, logistics and mobility will ask what this means for them.
know: Over 60% of humanoid shipments still go to entertainment, performances and research data collection, not factory work.
A pilot that contributes to production is not the same as a robot replacing a worker one-for-one. Productivity data is still limited.

qa.q: Will humanoids replace factory workers soon?
qa.a: Not at scale yet. Expect them first in repetitive, hard-to-staff tasks, alongside people.

qa.q: Why human shape rather than specialised machines?
qa.a: Because factories, warehouses and homes are built for humans; a human-shaped robot can use them without redesign.

deep.plain: Language models learned from text, so they’re good with words but have no feel for how the physical world works. A world model learns how things move, fall, collide and react, like a child who learns that a glass falls and breaks. Once an AI can simulate the world, a robot can practise a million times in a virtual space before touching anything real, and a factory can test a new line before building it.

terms.def: An AI that predicts how a physical scene will change over time: space, motion, cause and effect.
A live virtual copy of a physical asset or process, used to test changes safely.
Designing and testing in a virtual environment before spending money in the real world.

going.lead: Gartner calls it a top trend
going.text: World models are #3 on Gartner’s 2027 list, with a forecast that 40% of robotics applications will use them by 2030, up from under 1% in 2025.

Google released Genie 4 in October 2026 for real-time interactive world simulation. NVIDIA launched Cosmos 3 as an open world model in June 2026 and added open driving and robotics versions on 5 November.
real-world motion data is scarce and expensive to collect. Simulation fills that gap, which is why world models and the humanoid boom go together.

deep.why: Industrial customers get simulation-first engineering: test a line, a warehouse or a process virtually before spending on it.
know: Simulations are only as good as their physics; what works in a virtual world can fail in a messy real one (the ‘sim-to-real gap’).
Most industrial use today is digital twins and planning, not fully autonomous robots.

qa.q: How is a world model different from ChatGPT?
qa.a: ChatGPT predicts the next word; a world model predicts what happens next in a physical scene.

qa.q: Where would a non-robotics company see this?
qa.a: Planning factory layouts, warehouses, energy networks or traffic flows by testing them in simulation first.

deep.plain: Normally scientists design an experiment, run it by hand, wait for results and decide what to try next. In a self-driving lab, AI proposes the next experiment, robots carry it out, and the result goes straight back to the AI to plan the next round, around the clock. It turns discovery from a slow craft into a fast loop. The first drugs designed this way are in clinical trials, but none has been fully approved yet.

terms.def: A lab where AI plans experiments and robots run them in a continuous loop.
Phase I tests safety, Phase II tests whether it works, Phase III confirms in large groups before approval.
A molecule whose structure was proposed or optimised mainly by AI models.

going.text: More than 173 AI-designed drug programmes were in clinical development in early 2026, up from about two dozen in late 2023.
As of mid-2026, no AI-discovered drug had full FDA approval; 15–20 programmes are due to report Phase III results in 2026–27. That is the real test.
AI-designed molecules pass early safety trials more often, but in Phase II they fail at about the same rate as conventional ones.
Danaher expects its first AI-powered autonomous research lab to operate at scale in early 2027.

deep.why: R&D cycles that took years can compress into weeks. Customers in life sciences, materials and chemicals will reorganise R&D around it.
know: Counts of AI drug programmes vary (117 to 200+) depending on what counts as ‘AI-designed’.
Faster discovery does not shorten the human trial stages, which still take years.

qa.q: So does AI make drugs faster or not?
qa.a: It speeds up finding and refining candidates. Proving they work in people still takes the usual trials.
The same loop applies to materials, batteries, chemicals and food science.

deep.plain: Most voice assistants work like a relay: first turn your speech into text, then think about the text, then turn the answer back into speech. A lot gets lost in that transcript: tone, hesitation, frustration. Speech reasoning models think directly on the sound, so they can hear that you’re upset or in a hurry and respond accordingly. Gartner expects them to take over most routine voice conversations in companies by 2030.

terms.def: The traditional chain of transcription, text reasoning and speech synthesis.
An AI that reasons directly on audio, keeping tone, timing and emotion.
An AI that holds a spoken conversation and takes actions, for example in a contact centre.

links.title: SecurityWeek: DeepMind and RSA-1024

deep.plain: Encryption protects everything from bank transfers to emails. One widely used method, RSA, relies on the fact that splitting a very large number into its factors is extremely hard. Google DeepMind’s AI agents, working with human cryptographers, found new and faster ways to attack an old, shorter version of it within weeks. Today’s standard keys are still safe, but the way security research is done has changed.

terms.def: A public-key encryption method based on the difficulty of factoring large numbers.
Longer keys are much harder to break; 1024-bit is considered obsolete.
New encryption designed to resist future quantum computers.

going.text: an AI-found signature-forgery method about 1,600x better in theory than the previous best for 1024-bit RSA, and a batch method making each additional 1024-bit key about 30x cheaper to factor.
when the agents re-ran a known attack, it used 3.5x less CPU time (391 vs 1,380 core-years).
two cooperating AI agents designed, coded and ran the attack with light human supervision, working with cryptographers from UC San Diego and Inria.

deep.why: Security assumptions now need regular re-testing at machine speed. Customers still running legacy keys have a reason to retire them.
know: Only obsolete 1024-bit RSA is affected. DeepMind says 2048-bit and larger keys remain secure.
The speed-ups are theoretical estimates.

qa.q: Is my bank account at risk?
qa.a: No; modern systems use stronger keys. Legacy systems with old keys should be retired.
